summary: Describes requirements for roaming among dial-up Internet providers, meaning the ability to use several ISPs while keeping a formal relationship with only one. It lists criteria for judging roaming protocols. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Roaming lets a dial-up customer sign in to Internet providers other than the one they pay. RFC 2477 lists what a roaming protocol has to be able to do, so that proposed protocols can be judged against the same list.

subtitle: What a dial-up roaming protocol has to do before it can be called standard

tldr.problem: Dial-up customers want to sign in to Internet providers other than the one they have an account with, and the roaming protocols used for that were growing in popularity with no agreed list of what they should do.
tldr.mechanism: The memo splits roaming into three subsystems, the phone book, authentication and accounting, and then lists requirements for each. A roaming standard must support PPP and IP, CHAP, dynamic address assignment, real-time accounting and hop-by-hop as well as end-to-end protection.
tldr.outcome: The memo is a checklist rather than a protocol: it says a submission that fails a must requirement is not compliant, one that meets all the musts but not all the shoulds is conditionally compliant, and one that meets everything is unconditionally compliant.

facts.label: Authentication methods
facts.value: CHAP must, EAP should, PAP should not be supported

today: RFC 2477 is an Informational memo that has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a checklist for judging proposed roaming protocols rather than a protocol itself, so it describes the shape a roaming system should have: a phone book, an authentication path and an accounting path.

sections.title: What Roaming Means Here
sections.content:
The memo defines roaming capability as the ability to use multiple Internet service providers while maintaining a formal customer-vendor relationship with only one. In other words, the user has an account with one provider and can also dial in to the others.

Operational roaming services were already providing worldwide roaming capability and growing in popularity, and the memo lists who was interested: regional providers operating within a state or province, wanting to combine their efforts with other regional providers to cover a wider area; national providers wanting to combine with providers in another nation to give coverage across a group of countries or a continent; and businesses wanting to offer employees a comprehensive package of dialup services worldwide, including Internet access and secure access to corporate intranets over a virtual private network.

The document is a set of requirements. It provides an architectural framework for provisioning roaming and describes the requirements that elements of that architecture must meet. The requirements are written to be used in evaluating protocol submissions, so the requirement words describe what a protocol must be able to do, and the protocol documents themselves decide whether a given feature is required, recommended or optional. A submission is not compliant if it fails one or more of the must or must-not requirements for a capability it implements. One that satisfies all the must and must-not requirements but not all the should or should-not requirements is said to be conditionally compliant, and one that satisfies them all is unconditionally compliant.
sections.plainLanguage: Roaming means a dial-up customer can sign in to Internet providers other than the one they pay. This memo lists what a roaming protocol has to be able to do, so that proposed protocols can be judged against the same list.

sections.title: The Three Subsystems
sections.content:
The roaming architecture has three major subsystems. The phone book subsystem maintains the user's phone book, which gives the location and phone numbers of the points of presence that are roaming enabled. The authentication subsystem gives authorized users access to those points of presence and denies access to unauthorized users. The accounting subsystem provides information on the resources used during the user's session.

The memo also fixes the vocabulary. The Network Access Server (NAS) is the device clients dial in to to get access to the network. An authentication server provides authentication and authorization within the roaming architecture, and an accounting server provides accounting. Either may be fronted by a proxy: an authentication proxy can forward authentication, implement policy, manage shared secrets and edit attributes, and to the NAS it appears to act as an authentication server while to the authentication server it appears to act as an authentication client. The accounting proxy plays the same double role for accounting, and can also improve reliability, support auditing and offer a pseudo-transactional capability.

One term matters for routing the packets. In order to route authentication and accounting packets, the user name presented to the NAS may contain structure, and that structure is the Network Access Identifier: it is the means by which the proxies work out which authentication or accounting server should receive the request.
sections.plainLanguage: The service has three parts: a phone book of access numbers, an authentication part that decides who gets in, and an accounting part that records what was used. Between the user's dial-in server and the provider that owns the account sit proxies, which pass requests along and can adjust them on the way.

sections.title: What the Phone Book Must Do
sections.content:
The phone book subsystem covers four things: phone number presentation, phone number exchange, phone book compilation and phone book update. Only one of them has to be standardised. Presentation, which shows the available numbers and lets the user choose one, depends on the connection management software, so vendors will differ and it need not be standardised. Exchange, the propagation of number changes between providers, need not be standardised at this time because current implementations do not automate it completely. Compilation, turning received updates into a new phone book, does not affect protocol interoperability and need not be standardised. Update, propagating the compiled phone book to users, does have to be standardised, so that providers can update user phone books independently of the client's software or operating system.

The update protocol must work across a range of platforms and operating systems without imposing operating system-specific requirements. The client must be able to determine the authenticity of the server sending the update, and the server may also authenticate the client. The protocol must be able to update from an arbitrary previous version to the latest available version, must let the client determine the integrity of the received update before applying it and of the newly produced phone book afterwards, and must be lightweight because the client may be a low-end machine or an Internet appliance. The mechanism must also support requesting that the phone book be transmitted in a particular language and character set, for example a Russian language phone book.

The phone book format has its own requirements. It must support the phone number attributes commonly used by providers, so that users know the capabilities of the available numbers, plus provider attributes describing the individual members of the roaming consortium and service attributes needed to configure the service. It must support the addition of phone number, provider and service attributes without modification to the update protocol, with registration of new attributes handled by IANA and enough attribute space to accommodate growth. And it must be compact, because the phone book is typically updated often and the format competes for bandwidth.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the phone book work can be left to each provider. The part that has to be the same everywhere is the way an updated phone book reaches the user, so that a provider can update it without caring what software the customer runs. That update has to be small, secure, able to jump from any old version to the newest, and able to carry the book in the customer's own language.

sections.title: Requirements for Authenticating Users
sections.content:
Connection management comes first. Because PPP is so popular and nearly everywhere, a roaming standard must support PPP and IP. It may support other framing protocols such as SLIP, though SLIP support is expected to prove difficult because SLIP does not support negotiation of connection parameters and lacks support for protocols other than IP. Support for non-IP protocols such as IPX or AppleTalk may be provided, since these may be useful for corporate intranet access over the Internet, but because the client will begin PPP negotiation immediately on connection, support for scripting should not be part of a roaming standard.

Identification needs a standardised format for the user ID and the realm presented to the NAS. For verification, a roaming standard must support CHAP and should support EAP, while PAP should not be supported because of security concerns, with a possible exception where PAP is used to support a one-time password or token. Because a roaming standard is likely to be widely deployed on the Internet, it must provide enough scalability to allow roaming associations with thousands of ISP members. It must also be able to incorporate RADIUS-enabled devices within the roaming architecture, which the memo expects to be accomplished with gateways between RADIUS and the roaming protocol.

Proxies in the path make two more demands. To ensure compatibility with the NAS or the local network, authentication and authorization proxies will often add, delete or modify attributes returned by the home authentication server, and will often carry out resource management and policy functions, so a roaming standard must support the ability of proxies to perform attribute editing and implement policy. For addressing, the standard must support dynamic address assignment, and may support static address assignment, most likely via layer 2 or layer 3 tunnelling. It must not preclude the use of layer 2 tunnelling protocols such as PPTP, L2F or L2TP, which hold great promise for implementing virtual private networks, and it must not preclude service providers provisioning Mobile IP Foreign Agents or other Mobile IP functionality.
sections.plainLanguage: A roaming protocol must let the customer connect the way dial-up normally works, using PPP and IP, and must prove who they are with CHAP, or better EAP, and not with a plain password. It has to work for groups of providers with thousands of members, and it has to let the proxies in the path adjust the answers they pass on, because that is how local rules get applied.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
A roaming standard must include a thorough security analysis, including a description of security threats and countermeasures, and this must include mechanisms for fraud prevention and detection. It must provide for hop-by-hop integrity protection and confidentiality, which may be accomplished through support of network layer security such as IPSEC.

End-to-end protection is also required, and for a specific reason. Because policy implementation and attribute editing are common in roaming systems, proxies may need to modify packets in transit between a local NAS and the home server. In order to permit authorized modifications while at the same time guarding against attacks by rogue proxies, it is necessary for a roaming standard to support data object security, which means end-to-end confidentiality and integrity protection on an attribute-by-attribute basis. Non-repudiation is explicitly not a requirement for a roaming standard.

The memo notes that, being a requirements document, it has no security concerns of its own; the security requirements it places on the protocols being evaluated are the ones described above.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol has to protect traffic on every hop and must be able to check that each attribute has not been altered. It must also explain how fraud would be prevented and spotted. One thing it does not have to do is prove afterwards who did what: non-repudiation is not required.

sections.title: Accounting Requirements
sections.content:
Real-time accounting is a practical necessity in today's roaming implementations, because it is what supports fraud detection and risk management, so a roaming standard must provide support for it.

There is no proposed standard for NAS accounting today, and there is wide variation in the protocols used by providers to communicate accounting information within their own organizations, so a roaming standard must prescribe a standardized format for accounting records. For the sake of efficiency, that record format must be compact.

The record format must also be able to encode the metrics commonly used to determine the user's bill. Since these metrics change over time, the format must be extensible so that future metrics can be added as they come along, and it must support both standard metrics and vendor-specific metrics.
sections.plainLanguage: The service has to keep track of what the customer used as it happens, so that fraud can be spotted and stopped. The records need a common shape, they need to be small, and they need room for new charges to be added later.
